metadata.title: Fluent Isn't Legitimate.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: an AI answer feels legitimate when it's fluent, but it only IS legitimate when someone is named to answer for it. Lands the carry-out that fluency and accountability are answers to two different questions, and only one of them is checkable.
metadata.anchor_pair: B01 -> B06 (two rooms, one identical AI answer: finance committee already legitimate via a named CFO, bedside fixed by naming the attending physician)

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes a confident-sounding AI answer is already trustworthy. But sounding right and being accountable are different things — the same answer can pass one and fail the other. So: confident, or accountable?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'The AI sounds confident. That means it's trustworthy. Right?', hesitates on 'trustworthy', corrects to 'accountable'

props.text:

Single-word trigger ('trustworthy') swapped for a single-word replacement ('accountable') so buildActs()'s whitespace-token match fires. beats.narration_text: Take one AI answer, word for word identical, and put it in two rooms: a finance committee reviewing a projection, and a hospital bedside where a clinician is deciding on a patient. In 1995 the sociologist Mark Suchman split 'legitimate' into three separate questions: does it serve the interest — pragmatic; is someone accountable — moral; does it just feel right, taken for granted — cognitive.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - two rooms, one identical AI answer, a three-box framework (PRAGMATIC / MORAL / COGNITIVE)

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - two rooms, one answer
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Two labeled rooms side by side, FINANCE COMMITTEE and HOSPITAL BEDSIDE, each holding an identical card reading the same AI answer text. Beside them, three stacked boxes appear one at a time: PRAGMATIC, MORAL, COGNITIVE. THIS EXACT TWO-ROOM COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B06.

beats.narration_text: The natural shortcut: if an answer reads fluently and sounds informed, all three questions feel already answered — it feels legitimate, so it must be.

shot.new_visual_element: The three boxes all lighting up at once, from fluency alone

production_viz.label: The natural guess - fluency answers everything
production_viz.mechanic: The same AI answer card, glowing softly to suggest fluency. A single arrow fans out from it to all three boxes (PRAGMATIC, MORAL, COGNITIVE) at once, each lighting up green in unison.

beats.narration_text: But fluency only ever answers the cognitive question. In the finance committee, the CFO owns the number, so moral legitimacy holds too. At the identical bedside sentence, no one is named to own it if it's wrong — moral legitimacy fails, even though it reads exactly the same.

shot.new_visual_element: The cognitive box stays lit in both rooms; the moral box goes dark only at the bedside

production_viz.label: The break - fluency only reaches cognitive
production_viz.mechanic: The B02 fan-out arrow is struck through in terracotta except the one line reaching COGNITIVE, which stays lit in both rooms. In the finance room, a small 'CFO' name tag appears beside MORAL, which lights up. In the bedside room, the MORAL box stays dark with an empty name-tag outline.

beats.narration_text: Which is why the fix isn't asking the AI to sound more careful — it's naming an accountable party and a review step before the answer is acted on. Name who signs off, and 'legitimate' stops being a feeling and starts being a checked fact.

shot.new_visual_element: A name and a review-step slot appearing beside the moral box, turning it from dark to lit

production_viz.label: The fix - name the accountable party first
production_viz.mechanic: The empty bedside name-tag outline from B03 fills in with a blank line labeled 'NAMED PARTY' and a second slot labeled 'REVIEW STEP', both appearing before an arrow pointing forward into a card reading 'ANSWER ACTED ON'. The MORAL box switches from dark to lit the moment both slots fill.

beats.narration_text: So an answer that feels natural and well-informed doesn't prove anyone is accountable for it — cognitive and moral legitimacy are answers to two different questions, and passing one says nothing about the other.

shot.new_visual_element: Cognitive box lit, moral box separately outlined and empty - no line connecting them

production_viz.label: A pass on cognitive proves nothing about moral
production_viz.mechanic: COGNITIVE box lit green, physically separated with no arrow connecting it to a dashed, empty outline of the MORAL box beside it. A small label beneath each reads 'feels right' and 'answers for it' — two separate questions, drawn with a visible gap between them.

beats.narration_text: And the reverse doesn't hold either: an answer that's hedged and clearly disclosed as AI-written still needs the same accountable party named — a disclaimer isn't a mechanism. Back to the two rooms: the finance committee already had a name attached, the CFO. Add that same one line to the bedside — the attending physician reviews and signs — and the identical AI answer becomes legitimate there too.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the bedside room's moral box fills in with a name, matching the finance room

production_viz.label: The anchor returns - the bedside room fixed
production_viz.mechanic: THE B01 TWO-ROOM COMPOSITION RETURNS, identical layout. A faded 'AI-DISCLOSED' label stamps onto the bedside card first, struck through — no change to its dark MORAL box. Then the same 'ATTENDING PHYSICIAN REVIEWS AND SIGNS' name tag used in B04 slides into the bedside room's empty slot, exactly matching the finance room's 'CFO' tag beside it. Both MORAL boxes now lit, both rooms fully legitimate.

beats.narration_text: An AI answer feels legitimate when it's fluent. It only is legitimate when someone is named to answer for it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. I want to run a legitimacy audit on an AI answer I'm about to act on, using Suchman's three types. Check: does it serve my actual interest — pragmatic; is a specific person or role named as accountable if it's wrong — moral; and am I trusting it because it sounds right, or because I can trace it — cognitive. Tell me which one is missing. Liam, in for Bear.
